evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University science education center
evidence.text: The article says the modern 凡-over-虫 form first occurs in Warring States Chu and Qin manuscripts. It traces the graph back to late Shang oracle-bone and early Western Zhou bronze forms identified as 鳳. Its proposed transition removes the bird body, retaining 凡 and tail-feather marks; the intermediate transition is inferred, since the article says it lacks examples from the proposed Western Zhou-to-Spring-and-Autumn interval. It describes Qin script as turning the feather strokes into 虫, the direct source of the seal-script form.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University science education center
evidence.text: The article reports late Shang oracle-bone divinations about whether wind would occur, including examples cited by inventory numbers 合13338, 合13347, 合13344 and 合10020. It therefore attests the wind word in use by the late Shang, while the written graph in those uses is discussed as the bird graph later identified with 鳳. The article also reports wind-intensity compounds and weather records. These examples establish the early wind sense, not the chronology of later figurative senses.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University science education center
evidence.text: The article analyzes the use of the bird graph for the wind word as a phonetic loan, motivated by wind's lack of a concrete shape. It says the words were close in Old Chinese: 風 has a labial initial in the 冬 group and 鳳 a related labial initial in the same group. However, the proposed original referent of the bird graph is only tentatively identified as green peafowl, and the article notes that clear oracle-bone examples of the graph meaning the animal are lacking or disputed. Thus the graphic-loan proposal does not independently establish the animal's original spoken name or pronunciation.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University science education center
evidence.text: For later forms, the article treats 凡 as the phonetic and the retained feather marks as graphic remnants of the bird graph, not as a verified semantic insect element. It reports that Chu forms preserve different parts of the feather design and that Qin forms reinterpret the lower feathers as 虫. This is an account of graphic development and corruption, separate from the early whole-graph loan.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.source: Shuowen Jiezi, quoted in CASE報科學; corroborated by Taiwan Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants listing the Shuowen entry
evidence.text: The Han-period Shuowen account defines 風 as the eight directional winds and explains it as 从虫凡聲, with an explanation that wind moves insects and insects transform after eight days. Modern paleographic accounts reject this insect explanation as a retrospective interpretation of the corrupted feather shape; it remains important evidence for how the graph was understood in the Han lexicographic tradition, not proof of its original construction.
evidence.title: 風 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 風 entry, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang 2003
evidence.text: The entry places 風 in the 凡 phonetic series and gives Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese forms 凡 *bom and 風 *plum/*plums. This supports a later 凡 phonetic role independently of the uncertain identity or pronunciation of the earlier bird referent. The initial and final differ in this reconstruction, so the entry's series analysis reflects historical phonetic relationships, not exact modern homophony.
evidence.title: 風 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart, supplementary Old Chinese reconstruction materials
evidence.text: The authors' official supplementary site identifies their 2014 book as the source for the reconstruction system. In the Baxter-Sagart system, the consulted table gives 風 wind as *prəm and its departing-tone reading as *prəm-s; modern Standard Mandarin is fēng and Guangzhou/Hong Kong Cantonese Jyutping is fung1. These readings do not by themselves establish the name of the bird depicted in early forms.
evidence.title: The Baxter-Sagart reconstruction of Old Chinese

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 風 entry, citing Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction
evidence.text: In the Baxter-Sagart system the entry supplies 風 *prəm and 凡 *bam, and reports 鳳 *bəm for the fenghuang word. This makes the historical relationship a near phonological match in that reconstruction, while not independently proving the depicted bird's name. The article's separate traditional category analysis says the initials are both labial and the rhyme group shared; systems and transcription conventions differ, so reconstructions should not be merged as if identical.
evidence.title: 風 - Wiktionary, the free dictionary

evidence.text: The consulted dictionary lists meanings including wind or moving air, teaching/custom, habits or prevailing climate, demeanor/style, trend/situation, news, scenery, and several further usages. The list does not establish when each sense arose or the semantic links among them; no dated sequence for these extensions was verified in this research.
evidence.title: 風 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.text: An older popular account says the wind deity graph became 鳳 and later separated into 風, with bird replaced by insect, and suggests 虫 might represent a dragon while acknowledging no settled explanation. This conflicts with the recent paleographic analysis that interprets 虫 as corruption of tail-feather strokes. The former is presented as an older explanatory account and is not stronger direct paleographic evidence.
evidence.title: 「風」という漢字の成り立ちを知りたいのですが……。

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University Science Education Center
evidence.text: The article says the modern graph with 虫 and 凡 first appears in Warring States Chu and Qin manuscripts. It traces the graph to late Shang oracle-bone and early Western Zhou bronze forms identified as 鳳. It proposes that bird details were dropped while 凡 and tail-feather marks remained; the transition interval between Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn is not represented by known examples in the article, so this intermediate stage is inferred. The article treats the late Shang use of the bird graph for the wind word as a whole-graph phonetic loan.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University Science Education Center
evidence.text: The article cites late Shang oracle-bone divinations about whether wind would occur, including inscriptions catalogued as 合13338, 合13347, 合13344 and 合10020. It reports that the wind sense was already in use by late Shang. It says the early bird graph may depict green peafowl, but clear uses of that graph for the animal are lacking or disputed. The wind-word reconstruction therefore does not independently establish the bird's spoken name or pronunciation.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.source: CASE報科學, National Taiwan University Science Education Center
evidence.text: The account treats 凡 as a phonetic in the later compound graph and the remaining marks as traces of the bird's tail feathers, not as an original insect semantic component. It describes Chu forms as preserving different parts of the feather design and Qin forms as reinterpreting the lower marks as 虫; this corrupted shape became the source of the seal-script form. This later sound component should be distinguished from the earlier proposal that the whole bird graph was borrowed for the wind word.
evidence.title: 甲骨文的「風」（鳳）與風神

evidence.text: The consulted entry lists 凡 as a sound-series member with Zhengzhang-style Old Chinese *bom, and 風 with *plum and *plums. It identifies 凡 as the phonetic in the later 風 graph. In the Baxter–Sagart table on that page, 風 has *prəm for the noun wind and *prəm-s for a departing-tone reading. Modern readings listed include Mandarin fēng and Guangzhou Cantonese Jyutping fung1. These are source-provided comparisons from distinct reconstruction systems; they do not identify the name of the early depicted bird.
evidence.title: 風 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.text: The page identifies 风 as the simplified form of 風 and reports Mandarin fēng. Its traditional-character dictionary material quotes the Shuowen explanation 从虫凡聲 and the account that wind moves insects and insects transform after eight days. It also quotes older textual senses beyond moving air, including teaching and customs, but the page does not provide a dated sequence establishing when those extensions arose or how they are linked.
evidence.title: 风 fēng、fěng - 漢典

evidence.text: The Commons file page identifies a vector drawing as a Western Zhou bronze-script 風 associated with the vessel 盠駒尊, gives the source as the uploader's own work, and labels the image in Japanese as a 風 graph on that vessel. The image is a modern redraw, not a photograph of the artifact. The page was returned in search results with reuse information, but opening it failed with a cache miss; the exact direct image URL and full license text could not be verified from an opened page, so this candidate is not selected.
evidence.title: File:風-bronze-2.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1
evidence.text: The official GSR-sorted table lists 凡 fán *[b]rom (in every case) and 風 fēng *prəm (wind (n.)). The brackets in 凡's form mark an uncertain segment in the authors' notation. These two forms belong to the Baxter–Sagart reconstruction system and should be compared separately from Zhengzhang's reconstructions.

gaps: The intermediate graphic forms proposed between early 鳳 and later 風 are explicitly not attested in the cited account for the proposed Western Zhou-to-Spring-and-Autumn interval; the sequence is a reconstruction.

The early bird graph's original referent and spoken name are not securely established. Green peafowl is proposed, but direct oracle-bone use for the animal is disputed or lacking; the wind-word reconstruction cannot independently prove the bird's name.

No independent primary publication of the cited oracle-bone inscriptions was opened; the modern article gives inscription catalogue identifiers and quoted readings, which are reported here as that author's account.

No reliable dated evidence was found for the order and semantic links among metaphorical senses such as customs, demeanor, trend, news, and style. Dictionary gloss lists alone do not establish chronology.
The full source image panels for early glyph forms were not visually inspected; historical shape descriptions here report the article's interpretation.

The repository's simplified-form claim that 风 arose by replacing 䖝 with 㐅 was not independently verified in the consulted sources. The sources opened here mainly address traditional 風 and do not establish the chronology or precise editorial pathway of 风.
The transition from the early 鳳-shaped graph to later 風 is an inferred reconstruction across a period for which the consulted paleographic account reports no intermediate examples.

The early bird graph's original referent and spoken name remain uncertain. Green peafowl is proposed, but animal-denoting oracle-bone attestations are disputed or lacking; the proposed whole-graph loan does not independently establish the bird's name or sound.
The late Shang wind examples are reported through a modern article that cites inscription catalogue numbers; no primary inscription catalogue page was independently opened in this invocation.
No dated sequence establishing the semantic extension from wind to teaching, customs, demeanor, style, trends or news was verified. A dictionary's gloss list is not a chronology.
No externally supported account was found for the specific simplified component pathway 䖝 → 㐅 in 风; the checked sources identify 风 as simplified from 風 but do not document that pathway.

Xiaoxuetang could not be accessed. The relevant Commons glyph file page was found but failed to open; no direct image URL or verified rights statement was secured. The other opened Commons file was a CC0 modern comparison chart that did not depict this character, so there is no selected image candidate.
